subject: humanities
passage: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa is the most famous painting in the world, and most visitors to the Louvre assume that its fame rests on its artistic qualities: the soft, smoky shading that blurs every edge, the mysterious half-smile, and the way the sitter's eyes seem to follow the viewer around the room.
passage_b: In the nineteenth century, the Mona Lisa was admired, but it was not more admired than many other paintings in the Louvre. That changed in 1911, when the painting was stolen from the museum and disappeared for two years. Newspapers around the world covered the theft, crowds lined up to stare at the empty space on the wall, and when the painting was recovered in 1913, it returned as a celebrity. Its qualities are real, but its fame owes at least as much to a crime.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that the painting was little known until it was stolen a second time
choices.B: By agreeing that the painting's fame rests entirely on its artistic qualities
choices.C: By arguing that a famous crime did as much as the painting's qualities to make it known
choices.D: By denying that the painting shows any unusual skill

explanation.why: Text 1 says visitors assume the painting's fame "rests on its artistic qualities." Text 2 says that before the 1911 theft it was "not more admired than many other paintings" and that its fame "owes at least as much to a crime." So the author of Text 2 would respond that the theft, not just the painting's qualities, explains its fame.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 describes only one theft, in 1911.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the fame owes at least as much to the theft, so its author would not agree.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 argues that the 1911 theft and the coverage it received made the painting a celebrity.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the painting's "qualities are real"; it questions only whether they explain its fame.
